title: The poem begins
hook: a sketchbook nobody was meant to see: a poet who says he wrote only for himself
tomorrow: a free Saturday slides away. what was it actually worth?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pali closed: a little Pali, not a password but a shared door into the chants and the people chanting them. Today a new block opens, and it's a poem.
screen: `A LITTLE PALI.` → `A NEW BLOCK: A POEM.`

segments.voice: Some of the best things people pass around were made for an audience of one: a grandmother's recipe notebook, a running playlist, a sketchbook nobody was supposed to open. They're honest because nobody was performing. The poem that opens this block starts the same way. Its author says, in the first verses, that he isn't writing for you. He's writing for himself. So why has anyone read it since?
screen: `MADE FOR AN AUDIENCE OF ONE.` → `A RECIPE NOTEBOOK, A SKETCHBOOK.` → `HE WROTE IT FOR HIMSELF. WHY READ IT?`

segments.voice: The poem is the Bodhicaryavatara, Shantideva's guide to the bodhisattva's way: how to live for others. You met him in year three as the monk his fellows thought was lazy, until he stood up and recited this. It's in Sanskrit, so it's dharma now, not dhamma. Two spellings, one word. In the opening verses, after his homage, Shantideva says nothing here is new, and he has no special skill with words. He wrote it, he says, to train his own mind. Then the turn: if someone with a makeup like his should come across it, it might help them too. That's the answer. A poem for living, written as practice, left open for anyone built the same way. Now the week behind us, six lines to carry in. Evam me sutam: thus have I heard. Sadhu, sadhu, sadhu. Strive on with care. Two spellings, one word. The whole chant. A little Pali. Each one a door. Shantideva's is next.
screen: `BODHICARYAVATARA: A GUIDE TO LIVING FOR OTHERS.` · `NOTHING NEW, HE SAYS.` · `WRITTEN TO TRAIN HIS OWN MIND.` · `SIX LINES FROM THE WEEK.` · then, large: `A POEM FOR LIVING.`

segments.voice: Read the three lines on the screen slowly, twice: Shantideva's opening, in plain words. Then close your eyes and let one of the week's six lines come and sit beside it. Stay with whichever one arrives.
screen: `NOTHING HERE IS NEW.` · `I MADE IT TO TRAIN MY OWN MIND.` · `IF SOMEONE LIKE ME SEES IT, MAY IT HELP.`

segments.voice: Bodhicaryavatara: Shantideva's poem on the way of awakening, how to live for others. Written for himself, left open for anyone.
Your line: a poem for living. Read as practice, the way it was written. One of fifty.

howItsDone: Mahayana Buddhists, and Tibetan Buddhists especially, study the Bodhicaryavatara verse by verse with a teacher, and its verses are recited in practice and quoted in talks.

fork.setup: your cousin forwards a 'Buddha quote' with a sunset and no source. which line from this week makes the kindest reply?

options: He wrote it to train his own mind, and hoped it would help someone like him. Like you.
It's a polite line. Old authors always pretend to be humble before the real advice.
Because it's a rulebook for monks, and ông hopes you'll ordain after school.
